item.title: Datasette Charts plugin updates improve hooks and adds documentation website
item.description:
Datasette Charts plugin updates improve hooks and adds documentation website

The datasette-charts plugin has released an update addressing friction points identified in its chart type plugin hooks, along with the launch of a dedicated documentation website.

🔍 Overview

The datasette-charts plugin features a hook system that allows other plugins to define new chart types. To test this functionality, Claude Opus 5.5 was used to build an experimental plugin, which revealed several friction points in the design. The current release addresses these issues to improve the development process for additional chart plugins.

⚙️ Key details

  • The release improves the ergonomics of building additional chart plugins.
  • Friction points identified by an experimental Claude Opus 5.5 plugin have been resolved.

🚀 Availability

  • A new website for the plugin is available at charts.datasette.io.
  • The website includes a tutorial for plugin authors.
  • A gallery displays core charts and annotations, with each item linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite.

#Datasette #Python #DataVisualization #Plugins #AIAssistedDevelopment

Source: Release: datasette-charts 0.4a0

item.title: Autumn-27 ARTEX Open-Source Fork Now Maintained by ChainReactors
item.description:
Autumn-27 ARTEX Open-Source Fork Now Maintained by ChainReactors

The Autumn-27/ARTEX project, an AI autonomous penetration testing system originally built with a Go backend and Next.js frontend, has seen its open-source continuation. The repository RuoJi6/ARTEX is a fork of the original Autumn-27/ARTEX, preserving the upstream commit history and AGPL-3.0 license. It is now maintained by ChainReactors.

🧩 How it works

The system integrates with external data sources to streamline asset collection. Specifically, it supports direct synchronization of asset data from ScopeSentry, eliminating the need for manual repeated collection. Users configure the ScopeSentry address and API key on the “Asset Sync” page, select targets and asset types (such as domains, subdomains, IPs, ports, sites, or endpoints) by project or task dimension, and import data to merge it into the ARTEX asset graph for agent exploration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Database & LLM: The system depends on PostgreSQL and requires an LLM configuration for exploration, supporting either ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY (configurable via CLI or UI).
  • MCP Support: Remote MCP can be configured in system settings using http (Streamable HTTP) or sse (legacy SSE).
  • Dockerization: The ruoji6/artex Docker image is built and published via GitHub Actions. It includes common tools like ripgrep, curl, vim, npm, and nmap. The image supports linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 architectures, with Docker automatically selecting the matching host architecture.
  • Persistence: The ./skills and ./data directories are persisted via bind mounts.

🚀 Availability

  • Docker Setup: The installation script automatically detects and installs Docker. Users can choose between “All Docker” (which generates a .env file and runs docker compose up -d) or local compilation.
  • Local Setup: For local runs, users select a database option, generate a config.json, and compile an embedded single binary.
  • Access: After installation, the service is accessible at http://localhost:8787, requiring an initial setup at /setup to set the admin password.
  • Download: Release packages are available for download from the repository’s Releases page. Linux ARM64 users (including ARM64 Kali) should select the linux-arm64 build, while x86_64 users select linux-amd64.
  • Execution: Users must launch the application using start.sh or start.bat rather than running ./artex directly. These scripts act as daemons that restart the program based on exit codes, which is required for the “one-click update” feature to function correctly.

#ARTEX #PenetrationTesting #OpenSource #SecurityTools #ChainReactors

Source: RuoJi6/ARTEX

item.title: Analysis of 5,400 Malicious NPM Packages Reveals Evolving Supply Chain Tactics
item.description:
Analysis of 5,400 Malicious NPM Packages Reveals Evolving Supply Chain Tactics

In this first part, we analyzed approximately 5,400 confirmed malicious npm packages published between December 2025 and October 2026, the first year following npm’s revocation of long-lived authentication tokens. The dataset comprises packages detected by a scanner that analyzes npm publish events for suspicious packages, with results filtered for precision by retaining only packages with at least one independent source, such as a public advisory, a vendor-published campaign report, an npm security takedown, or analyst review. Time is measured by npm publish date, and the unit of record is the package version, dated by its first malicious version.

🔍 Threat Landscape Overview

Monthly counts of confirmed malicious packages vary by a factor of fifteen across the period. Activity remains stable with several hundred new publisher accounts per month and a flat rate of malicious packages relative to total packages published. In August 2026, a single dependency-confusion campaign accounts for 78% of confirmed versions. Dependency-confusion reconnaissance is continuous, present in every month at a consistent level, while compromise of legitimate packages is episodic.

🧩 Attack Vectors and Campaigns

Three waves of a single worm family occurred in May, June, and August 2026. The May and August waves each compromised more than one hundred packages, and the June wave republished a vendor’s entire scope in one day.

  • Token Theft Shift: Classic long-lived tokens were revoked on December 9, 2025. Theft of npm authentication tokens peaked at 22% of packages in March 2026 and fell below 5% from May. The tokens targeted in this period were plausibly granular access tokens and CI secrets.
  • Obfuscation: The share of actors whose packages trigger an obfuscation rule more than doubled between May and August 2026. 72% of packages have an obfuscation marker, and 30% retrieve a second stage.
  • Compromised Packages: 78% of compromised versions add or modify a lifecycle script, compared with 4% of attacker-created packages. 23% show a change of maintainer or publisher, but the majority of compromises are published through the legitimate account and leave ownership records unchanged.

⚙️ Attacker Profile and Package Characteristics

99% of malicious packages are published by single-maintainer accounts, and 55% of accounts use a free-mail address. Two-thirds of accounts publish exactly one malicious package; among those publishing more than one, the median interval from first to last malicious publish is under one day.

  • DPRK-nexus Campaigns: These are the exception, operating several hundred accounts at one to two packages each, with 83% on free-mail addresses.
  • Other Named Campaigns: These use free-mail addresses in 15% of cases, consistent with procured account pools.
  • Package Traits: 88% of packages are under thirty days old at the malicious publish, 75% declare no repository, and 65% retain npm init template values in the author, description, or repository fields. 54% declare a lifecycle script, and 17% carry an internal-looking name (core, utils, sdk, config). Typosquatting is a minority tactic, with 13% embedding a popular package name and under 5% being within two character edits of one.

💡 Payload Behavior and Targeting

Credential and data theft is the predominant behavior in every month, except August. In August, a significant number of packages stole credentials but ultimately aimed to deliver a Sliver command-and-control implant on the victim machine, changing their classification to Trojan / Downloader.

  • Credential Targets: 45% of credential stealers target a single credential class, while 36% target three or more. Single-class stealers are distributed evenly across cloud credentials, SSH keys, AI-developer credentials, npm tokens, and .env files. In multi-class stealers, cloud credentials, SSH keys, and .env files co-occur; wallet and browser-data theft occur separately.
  • AI Developer Credentials: Targeting remained at 1-4% of packages throughout the year, but absolute counts rose with volume. AI-developer credentials are the most specialized target: 80% of packages that target them target no other class.
  • OS Specificity: 55% of packages contain no operating-system-specific code. Droppers target Windows (PowerShell, scheduled tasks, executables), while credential stealers and backdoors target Linux (systemd, cron, shell configuration files). macOS-specific code appears in approximately one in eight stealers.
  • Scoped Packages: 24% of packages are scoped, across more than three hundred distinct scopes, most of which contain a single malicious package.

#npmSecurity #SupplyChainAttack #MalwareAnalysis #ThreatIntelligence #OpenSource

Source: What 5,400 Malicious npm Packages Reveal about Software Supply Chain Risk in 2026

item.title: ROS 2 Packages Integrate llama.cpp for LLM and VLM Support
item.description:
ROS 2 Packages Integrate llama.cpp for LLM and VLM Support

A new set of ROS 2 packages has been released to integrate the llama.cpp library into ROS 2 environments. This repository allows developers to incorporate llama.cpp’s optimization capabilities into ROS 2 projects to run various machine learning models.

🧩 How it works

The llama_ros packages enable the execution of GGUF-based models within a ROS 2 framework. The supported model types include:

  • Large Language Models (LLMs)
  • Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
  • Audio-language models
  • Embedding models
  • Reranking models

⚙️ Key details

Beyond basic model execution, the packages provide specific interfaces and features derived from llama.cpp:

  • An OpenAI-compatible chat completions interface that supports tool calling, reasoning, and streaming.
  • Speculative decoding.
  • Support for decision models, including OpenJEV, Lev, Kev, Nimble, Laya, and Clef.
  • Grammar-based generation (GBNF).
  • Real-time modification of LoRAs.

#ROS2 #llama.cpp #LLM #ROS #GenerativeAI

Source: mgonzs13/llama_ros

item.title: AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability
item.description:
AgnostUI Local v2 copies UI components into your project for AI readability

AgnostUI Local (v2) is a new CLI-based UI component library that copies components directly into your project at install time. Instead of keeping components hidden inside node_modules, the source code lands directly in your repository, providing full control and native integration with your framework.

🧩 How it works

AgnostUI components are authored as Lit Web Components, a standards-based layer over native Custom Elements. The CLI wraps these components for your specific framework at copy time. By default, components are placed under src/components/ag/, creating a dedicated namespace that keeps AgnosticUI components separate from your own code. This approach ensures that your design system does not fork when your tech stack changes.

🤖 AI and Agent Integration

Because the component source lives locally, it is readable by AI tools such as Cursor, Claude, Copilot, Windsurf, Aider, Gemini, Replit, Kiro, and Antigravity. Every tool sees the raw source, creating a high-fidelity environment for Generative UI and agent-driven interfaces.

  • Reduce Hallucination: Since the LLM reads local files like any other code, it knows exactly what is possible, preventing invented props or APIs.
  • Better Token Efficiency: Using semantic HTML and standard CSS provides clean context, allowing agents to spend fewer tokens to understand the UI for faster, more accurate generations.
  • Agent Skills: AgnosticUI Playbooks act as pre-defined skills, prompting agents to scaffold complex, accessible workflows using local components.

📜 Playbooks and Components

The schema-driven layer ships with three companion documents. AgnosticUI offers Playbooks that demonstrate modular, prompt-driven UI components. These Playbooks support agent-generated UI workflows directly.

Playbook Name Description
Login Form Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Onboarding Wizard Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Discovery Dashboard Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Support Center Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Data Grid Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Blog / Article Reader Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components
Landing / Marketing Page Demonstrates modular, prompt-driven UI components

💡 Why it matters

AgnostUI Local solves the “Black Box” problem of traditional libraries hidden in node_modules. It is designed as the architecture for the next era of development, characterized as context-aware, framework-agnostic, and AI-ready.

#AIagents #UILibraries #WebDevelopment #LitWebComponents #CodeGen #DesignSystems

Source: AgnosticUI/agnosticui

item.title: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 Released as Production-Ready Successor to Semantic Kernel
item.description:
Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 Released as Production-Ready Successor to Semantic Kernel

Semantic Kernel is now Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF), the enterprise-ready successor designed for building AI agents and multi-agent systems. MAF is now available at version 1.0 as a production-ready release, featuring stable APIs and a commitment to long-term support.

🧩 Core Capabilities

Microsoft Agent Framework is a model-agnostic SDK that empowers developers to build, orchestrate, and deploy AI agents. Key features include:

  • Multi-Agent Orchestration: Orchestrate complex workflows with collaborating specialist agents, suitable for both single assistants and fleets of specialized agents.
  • Model Support: Connect to any LLM with built-in support for OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Hugging Face, and NVidia.
  • Modular Design: Build modular AI agents with access to tools/plugins, memory, and planning capabilities.
  • Input Processing: Process text, vision, and audio inputs.
  • Local Execution: Run with Ollama, LMStudio, or ONNX.
  • Workflow Modeling: Model complex business processes with a structured workflow approach.

⚙️ Integration and Extensibility

The framework supports cross-runtime interoperability via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP). Developers can extend agents using:

  • Native code functions
  • Prompt templates
  • OpenAPI specifications
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP)

It offers seamless integration with Azure AI Search, Elasticsearch, Chroma, and other data sources.

🚀 Platform Requirements

Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 is built for observability, security, and stable APIs, with the following platform support:

Language/Platform Version Requirement
Python 3.11 through 3.14
.NET .NET 10.0+
Java JDK 17+
Operating Systems Windows, macOS, Linux

#MicrosoftAgentFramework #SemanticKernel #AIagents #MultiAgentSystems #LLM

Source: microsoft/semantic-kernel

item.title: 🚀 Supercharge Your Coding: How Cursor AI & MCP Are Revolutionizing Development
item.description:
🚀 Supercharge Your Coding: How Cursor AI & MCP Are Revolutionizing Development

𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮: Discover how Cursor AI’s intelligent code editor combined with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) creates a powerful development environment that streamlines coding, enhances productivity, and makes advanced AI accessible to developers of all skill levels.

🧠 Intelligent Coding Assistants: The Future is Here

Remember when coding meant staring at a blank screen, hoping for inspiration? Those days are rapidly disappearing as AI-powered coding tools transform how we write, debug, and deploy software. Two revolutionary technologies—Cursor AI and the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—are at the forefront of this transformation, promising to make developers more efficient while lowering the barrier to entry for AI-enhanced development.

But what exactly are these tools, and why should you care? Let’s explore how they work together to create a seamless, intelligent coding environment that might just change the way you approach your next project.

🖥️ Cursor AI: Your Intelligent Coding Companion

Cursor AI isn’t just another code editor—it’s your personal coding assistant integrated directly into your development environment. Think of it as having an experienced developer looking over your shoulder, offering suggestions, catching errors, and helping you write cleaner code faster.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗖𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁:

  • 🔍 Code Autocompletion: Get real-time suggestions as you type, significantly boosting your productivity

  • 🐛 Error Detection: Automatically identifies potential bugs and issues before they become problems

  • 🔄 Code Refactoring: Simplifies and optimizes your code with minimal effort, ensuring maintainability

  • 📝 Documentation Assistance: Automatically generates code comments and explanations, saving you time

Setting up Cursor AI is refreshingly straightforward. Simply visit the official website, download the installer for your operating system, and follow the guided installation process. Within minutes, you’ll have access to a sleek, modern interface designed to make coding more intuitive and efficient.

🔄 MCP: The Context Bridge for AI Tools

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), developed by Anthropic, serves as the critical bridge between your code and its data sources. This standardized interface ensures that your AI models have the context they need to make informed decisions and provide accurate responses.

𝘞𝘩𝘺 𝘋𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘭𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘈𝘳𝘦 𝘌𝘹𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘈𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘔𝘊𝘗:

  • 🧩 Context Management: Ensures AI models have access to the contextual information they need

  • 🔌 Plug-and-Play Integration: Eliminates complex configuration requirements

  • 📈 Enhanced Model Performance: Improves results, especially in natural language processing tasks

  • 🔄 Flexibility: Adapts to various data sources, structuring context to facilitate better learning and inference

The integration process is surprisingly simple. First, find an MCP server on platforms like Smithery AI, then copy the installation command. Within Cursor AI, navigate to settings, add a new MCP server, paste the command, and you’re ready to go.

🛠️ Creating a Powerful Workflow with Cursor AI and MCP

When combined, Cursor AI and MCP create a development environment that’s greater than the sum of its parts. Here’s what this powerful pairing offers different types of users:

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗡𝗲𝘄𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀:

The user-friendly interface and guided integration process make advanced AI accessible without requiring deep expertise. You’ll spend less time struggling with setup and more time learning and building.

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀:

Enhanced productivity through better context management and streamlined workflows means you can develop and test applications faster than ever before.

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀:

Teams benefit from greater efficiency, more consistent project outcomes, and robust testing capabilities, making these tools ideal for business environments where quality and speed matter.

Let’s see this in action. After configuring MCP with Cursor AI, you can test the integration by running a context-aware function. For example, using the “Sequential-Thinking MCP” to plan a game development project would result in a structured approach covering game concept, technical requirements, and game elements—without writing a single line of code yet.

🔗 Enhancing Your Stack with Apidog

While Cursor AI and MCP focus on improving your coding experience, adding Apidog to your toolkit can significantly enhance your API development and documentation workflow. This all-in-one platform offers powerful tools for designing, testing, and documenting APIs in a unified environment.

By incorporating Apidog alongside Cursor AI and MCP, you create a comprehensive development ecosystem that addresses every aspect of modern application development—from writing code to deploying and documenting APIs.

🌟 The Future of Development Is Here

The combination of Cursor AI and MCP represents a significant leap forward in how we approach software development. These tools don’t just make coding faster—they make it smarter, more accessible, and more enjoyable.

As AI continues to evolve, we can expect these tools to become even more sophisticated, further blurring the line between human and machine capabilities. The result? More intuitive coding experiences, fewer errors, and greater innovation across the development landscape.

The question isn’t whether you should adopt these technologies—it’s how quickly you can integrate them into your workflow to stay ahead of the curve. Are you ready to embrace the future of development?
